claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by a chromium–molybdenum oxide passive film.
The governing passive film is thin, stable, and self-healing.
The chromium–molybdenum oxide film limits penetration by aggressive ions and localizes defects.
Steels typical of the stated applications contain approximately 10–20% chromium and 1–3% molybdenum.
Mechanical polishing or chemical etching can alter or partially disrupt the initial oxide layer.
Changing chromium and molybdenum content changes their availability for passive-film formation.
Chromium and molybdenum enrich near the steel surface under operational conditions.
Surface-enriched chromium and molybdenum form the passive oxide film.
The passive film acts as a barrier against corrosive species.
The passive film provides a self-repairing interface against corrosive species.
Reduced ion penetration and localized film breakdown lower the corrosion rate relative to steels with compromised or thinner films.
Specimens retaining robust passive films will have lower weight-loss corrosion rates than specimens with disrupted films or lower chromium and molybdenum levels.
Specimens retaining robust passive films will exhibit less pit formation than specimens with disrupted films or lower chromium and molybdenum levels.
Specimens retaining robust passive films will exhibit more stable electrochemical impedance measurements than specimens with disrupted films or lower chromium and molybdenum levels.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply within approximately 10–20% chromium and 1–3% molybdenum under normal chemical-processing and nuclear-power operating environments.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to steels with substantially different alloying elements or to environments outside typical temperature, pH, and chloride ranges.
